name: Huastec, San Luís Potosí
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Según los ejemplos de (a), el huasteco no distingue entre las sílabas CV y CVC para la asignación del acento, ambos tipos funcionan de la misma manera. Esto quiere decir que las consonantes en coda no contribuyen al peso de la sílaba. El patrón acentual es fuerte-débil, por lo que corresponde a un patrón trocaico. En los ejemplos de (b) apreciamos que la lengua es sensible a la cantidad, ya que si hay una sílaba con vocal larga, ésta atrae el acento. La prominencia acentual de las palabras fonológicas se basa en los tres tipos de pies trocaicos de (18): un pie constituido por dos sílabas, por una sílaba pesada o bien una sola sílaba para los monosilábicos (Kager 2007).
new_statements.translation: According to the examples in (a) ['ka.le 'jump!', 'ka.mab 'tooth', 'pak.laθ 'folded'], Huastec does not distinguish CV from CVC syllables for stress assignment; both types behave the same way. This means that coda consonants do not contribute to syllable weight. The stress pattern is strong-weak, i.e. trochaic. In the examples in (b) [pa.'t'aal 'iron', 'kuu.lab 'mixture', 'laab.lij 'to bless', tek'.'θaal 'to cook', tsa.ma.'maal 'very cold', wa.'k'aaʃ 'to get each other wet'] we see that the language is quantity-sensitive: if there is a syllable with a long vowel, it attracts the stress. The stress prominence of phonological words rests on the three kinds of trochaic feet in (18): a foot made of two syllables, of one heavy syllable, or of a single syllable for monosyllables (Kager 2007).

The saved page image shows the same text and the stress marks in Tabla 22b (pa.'t'aal, 'kuu.lab, 'laab.lij, tek'.'θaal, tsa.ma.'maal, wa.'k'aaʃ); Tabla 22a on p. 274 has 'ka.le, 'ka.mab, 'pak.laθ as the report renders them. Reading: I read pp. 272-281 (the whole 'Patrón acentual' section plus the chapter conclusion). Only vowel length adds weight (p. 274-275: onsets and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive, left-edge trochaic stress at the word level: only vowel length makes a syllable heavy (coda consonants are weightless), a syllable with a long vowel takes the stress wherever it sits in the word (pa.'t'aal, tsa.ma.'maal), and words without a long vowel are stressed on the first syllable ('ka.le, 'ka.mab, 'pak.laθ). The source's data have at most one long vowel per word, so it does not decide between 'rightmost' (Larsen & Pike 1949 as rendered by Hagberg 1993 and Bennett 2016) and 'first' long vowel (Kondic 2012) for words with two; Bennett 2016:496 notes this chapter has 'apparent counter-examples' to the rightmost-long-vowel rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress is described. The source reports two primary stresses in abstract nouns formed with -tal-aab ('hi.lij.ta.'laab 'sourness', '?i.nik.ta.'laab 'manliness', pp. 279-280) and analyses them as two phonological words; the suffix complex -talaab attracts its own stress on its long vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds follow the same pattern (Tabla 23, p. 279: 'Ti/ 'trunk', tsi.'jook 'chin'). The -tal-aab formations with double primary stress are treated as two prosodic words rather than as exceptions. Larsen 1955 (vocabulary, same Tancanhuitz area) marks no stress at all.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word level ('patrón acentual a nivel léxico', p. 274), elicited forms with instrumental durations; the chapter also states (p. 235) that the accent study is based on the Potosino variety. Meléndez 2017:36 (Veracruz) adds, citing Larsen & Pike 1949 for San Luis Potosí, that stress is not phonological (contrastive) but rule-predictable.
new_statements.identity_note: huas1255 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO 639-3 code [hva] 'San Luís Potosí Huastec', merged into [hus] Huastec by change request 2008-051 (effective 2009-01-16); it is the Potosino dialect of Huastec / Tének, Glottolog huas1242 (Mayan, Huastecan), which the catalog already carries (Kondic 2012 for the South Eastern/Veracruz variety, with Herrera Zendejas 2014 noted as refining it). The deciding source quoted here, Herrera Zendejas 2014 ch. 7, describes the Tancanhuitz (San Luis Potosí) variety, i.e. exactly the lect this retired code named; Larsen 1955 and Larsen & Pike 1949 are also Tancanhuitz-area Potosino. Meléndez 2017 (El Mamey, Tantoyuca) and Kondic 2012 (Chontla/South Eastern) describe the Veracruz varieties (the sibling retired code huas1256 = hsf). The catalog owner may prefer to fold this key into huas1242 rather than carry a separate row.

new_statements.quote: [p. 269, sec. 3:] Intonation and stress are both described in terms of a point in the word which is designated as the POTENTIAL CONTOUR POINT. This is located on the last long vowel of the word, or, if there are no long vowels in the word, on the first short vowel, regardless of the number of vowels in the word. [p. 274, sec. 6:] The stress of any word not in phrase-final position is predictable: it coincides with the potential contour point (§3), and thus depends on the sequence of long and short vowels in the word. [p. 277, sec. 10:] Stress in Huasteco is considered to be non-phonemic because (1) the placement of stress in any word that is not phrase-final can be predicted from the shape of the word itself
new_statements.citation: Larsen, Raymond S. & Eunice V. Pike. 1949. Huasteco intonations and phonemes. Language 25(3): 268-277.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record for huas1255; the existing statement (Herrera Zendejas 2014:275, Tancanhuitz SLP) reads weight-sensitive with a trochaic strong-weak pattern, codas inert, long vowels attracting stress. Larsen & Pike 1949 agree on type (weight-sensitive, vowel length only, codas irrelevant) and add the explicit placement rule: rightmost long vowel, otherwise the first syllable regardless of word length; stress non-phonemic and subordinate to an intonation system; proclitics and compound first members unstressed; a limited phrase-final fluctuation conditioned by intonation contour. Same Potosino variety (community c. 40 miles north of Tamazunchale, SLP, fn. 3 p. 268).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-phonemic and fully predictable from vowel length: it falls on the last (rightmost) long vowel of the word; if the word has no long vowel, on the first vowel, whatever the number of syllables (formulas p. 269: SS, LS, SL, LL; SSS, LSS, SLS, LLS, SSL, LSL, LLL with the stressed syllable being the last L, else the first S). Proclitics (pronominal ?u-, ?in-, ?an- etc.) and unstressed first members of compounds joined by a hyphen are not counted. Stress on phrase-initial or -medial words is weaker than on the phrase-final word; the phrase-final stress normally sits on the same point (the 'routine contour point'), where the intonation contour begins. Coda consonants play no role; only vowel length counts. Pitch is intonational (three levels, ten-odd contours), not lexical tone (secs. 4-5, 10).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Proclitics 'are never stressed and.. not included in the contrastive intonation contours' (p. 274); first members of phonemic compounds are likewise unstressed (?oš-?inik 'orphan'), whereas morphological compounds written with a dash 'are stressed as two words' (pa·le?–c'ili? 'a certain type of grasshopper', p. 274). Non-final words carry a less intense stress than the phrase-final word.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 274: in phrase-final words ending in a short vowel spoken with the mid-high, low-high, low-mid or mid-mid intonation contours 'the stress appears to fluctuate between the final syllable and the contour point': //bakan// ['bakan] or [ba'kan] 'tortilla', //?uča·štik// 'conversationalist'. p. 272 (sec. 5.4): under the call contour the last vowel may be lengthened, shifting the contour point (hence stress) to it (katarina ~ katari·na). Spanish loans (rika·rdo, hose·) take the same system (p. 276). Non-phonemic: 'there is still no contrast between words differently stressed' (p. 277).
new_statements.identity_note: Larsen & Pike 1949 fn. 3 (p. 268): 'Huasteco is a Mayan language spoken in the states of San Luis Potosi and Vera Cruz, Mexico. The dialect described in this paper is that of Oto[ñ]iel Oyarvide, an Indian community about 40 miles north of Tamazunchale, San Luis Potosi' (scanned reads 'Otofiiel Oyarvide'); informants Tomás Martínez, José Santiago, Juana Hernández, c. 20 years old; Larsen's field trips 1942-1948, Pike's September-October 1948; Pike is responsible for the analysis of intonation, stress and vowel length. This is the Potosino variety = huas1255 (retired ISO hva), the same variety as Herrera Zendejas 2014 (Tancanhuitz, SLP) behind the existing statement. Norcliffe 2003 is a Proto-Huastecan (Huastec + Chicomuceltec) reconstruction, not a description of one dialect.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction among the sources opened. Larsen & Pike 1949 (Otoñiel/Oyarvide-area community north of Tamazunchale, SLP) and the existing Herrera Zendejas 2014 statement (Tancanhuitz, SLP) both make Huastec stress quantity-sensitive on vowel length with codas inert; Larsen & Pike state the default more sharply (last long vowel, else the FIRST vowel of the word, however long the word), whereas Herrera Zendejas 2014 models it as moraic trochees with a strong-weak default. The one point of tension is second-hand: our earlier reading note on this folder's records that Herrera Zendejas 2014:281 reports unanalysed stress shifts in words without long vowels ([wi.le] vs [wi.le.lom], [ʔo.hob] vs [ʔo.ho.be]), and Bennett 2016:496 calls these 'apparent counter-examples' to the Larsen & Pike/Edmonson/Herrera Zendejas 2011 rule; Larsen & Pike themselves only allow phrase-final fluctuation toward the final syllable under four specific intonation contours. Herrera Zendejas 2011 and Norcliffe 2003 could not be opened, so nothing from them is asserted.
